questions.question_text: A 22-year-old female recently diagnosed with schizophrenia is started on an antipsychotic medication
What is the �rst line medication for a patient newly diagnosed with mild-moderate Lewy Body Dementia?
questions.explanation:
The NICE guidelines state the following: O�er donepezil or rivastigmine to people with mild to moderate dementia with Lewy Bodies. Only
consider galantamine for the above patient group if donepezil or rivastigmine are not tolerated. Consider memantine for people with
dementia with Lewy bodies if AChE inhibitors are not tolerated or are contraindicated. Trazadone is an antidepressant and not a �rst line
treatment for dementia. Quetiapine is not indicated as there are no psychotic symptoms reported, and even if there were, an AChE inhibitor
would be the �rst line of treatment. (Reference: Dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their
carers. NICE guideline [NG97] Published date: June 2018. non-cognitive-symptoms)

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a core feature of dementia with Lewy bodies?
questions.explanation:
In addition to cognitive decline (dementia), a patient with probable Dementia with Lewy Bodies (DLB) must also have at least two “core
clinical features" which includes: cognitive �uctuations, visual hallucinations, rapid eye movement (REM) sleep behaviour disorder, and
parkinsonism. Other features such as antipsychotic sensitivity, falls, hallucinations in other modalities, delusions, anxiety and depression
may be supportive but are not core features. (Ref: Farlow RF, DeKosky ST, Eichler AF. (2018) Clinical features and diagnosis of dementia with
Lewy bodies.

questions.question_text:
Mabel is 82 years old and lives alone. She has recently been diagnosed with late onset schizophrenia (or paraphrenia). Which ONE of the
following symptoms are more commonly found in late onset schizophrenia when compared to adult onset schizophrenia?
questions.explanation:
A few studies have compared early onset and late onset schizophrenia (previously known as paraphrenia) with adult onset schizophrenia
identifying signi�cant di�erences in phenomenology and symptomatology. Persecutory delusions and partition delusions are more common
in late onset schizophrenia. Catatonia, thought insertion and withdrawal are more common in young onset as are negative symptoms such
as blunting of a�ect. Formal thought disorder is also more common in younger age groups. (Ref: Howard R, Castle D, Wessely S, Murray R. A
comparative study of 470 cases of early-onset and late-onset schizophrenia. The British journal of psychiatry. 1993 Sep;163(3):352-7)

questions.question_text:
Miss Laura Brookes is a 55-year-old woman who has been diagnosed with REM sleep disorder due to excessive movements during sleep.
Which of the following is this diagnosis associated with?
questions.explanation:
REM sleep behavioural disorder is characterized by patients acting out their dreams during REM sleep and involves the loss of normal
muscle tone during this phase of sleep. It is strongly associated with later development of synucleopathies, such as Parkinson's disease and
Lewy Body Dementia.

questions.question_text:
Depression is commonly co-morbid with dementia but can be more di�cult to identify in patients with clinically signi�cant cognitive
impairment. Which of the followings are most useful for detecting depression in people with dementia?
questions.explanation:
The Cornell Scale for Depression in Dementia is designed for the assessment of depression in older people with dementia who can at least
communicate basic needs. It has been tested for reliability, sensitivity and validity on patients in community, hospital and care home
settings. Scores are determined by a combination of prior observation and two interviews: 20 minutes with the carer and 10 minutes with
the patient.

questions.question_text:
You have just diagnosed Mr Jackson with mixed Alzheimer's and vascular dementia in the memory clinic. His daughter phones you
afterwards to inquire about risk factors she might address to reduce her chance of developing dementia. Which ONE of the following
statements is INCORRECT with regards to associations with dementia?

options.text: Late life depression associated with increased risk of all types of dementia
Reduced frequency of social contacts associated with increased risk of all types of dementia
Rural living associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's dementia
Obesity associated with increased risk for Alzheimer's dementia
Type 2 diabetes associated with increased risk of vascular dementia

correct_answer.text: Rural living associated with increased risk of Alzheimer's dementia

questions.explanation:
A recent review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses examined associations between 76 factors and dementia. Seven associations
presented convincing evidence. These were benzodiazepine use, depression at any age, late life depression, frequency of social contacts for
all types of dementia. Type 2 diabetes was associated with vascular dementia and Alzheimer's disease. Obesity has previously been
associated with Alzheimer's dementia. Rural living was found to not be signi�cant in terms of association with dementia of any type. (Ref:
Bellou V, Belbasis L, Tzoulaki I, Middleton LT, Ioannidis JP, Evangelou E. Systematic evaluation of the associations between environmental risk
factors and dementia: An umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses. Alzheimer's & Dementia. 2017 Apr 1;13(4):406-18.)

questions.question_text: Regarding suicide in later life, which ONE of the following interventions is correctly matched to its type of preventative strategy?

options.text: Education program to improve GP's ability to treat depression – universal prevention
ECT for inpatients with psychotic depression – selective intervention
Restriction of lethal means of suicide – indicated prevention
Proactive screening for depression and pain management in older adults in primary care with poorly controlled pain – selective
Peer companionship and befriending programs for isolated older people – universal prevention

questions.explanation:
Universal prevention aims to reduce incidence at whole community or society levels. Selective prevention targets groups who do not
currently have suicidal ideation but are vulnerable due to life circumstances or demonstrate risk factors for depression and suicide.
Indicated prevention focusses on individuals who are in imminent danger of attempting suicide, have recently done so, or express suicidal
thoughts. Restriction of lethal means is a universal prevention. Education programs to improve GP's treatment is a selective prevention as it
focusses on patients who are already diagnosed with depression. Peer companionship for isolated older people is a selective intervention as
it targets lonely people who are at higher risk of suicide. ECT for inpatients with psychotic depression is an indicated prevention strategy as it
targets those who are high risk of suicide. Proactive screening for depression of older adults with uncontrolled pain is a selective
intervention as it targets a group who do not necessarily have depression but have pain which is a risk factor for developing depression and
attempting suicide. (Ref: Lapierre S, Erlangsen A, Waern M, De Leo D, Oyama H, Scocco P, et al. A systematic review of elderly suicide
prevention programs. Crisis. 2011;32(2):88-98)

questions.question_text:
Mr Jones is a 65-year-old man who is brought to A&E with a sudden onset of severe headache, vomiting, and dizziness, after having had a
brief loss of consciousness whilst in the supermarket. He has a pacemaker and history of hypertension. Which investigation would be the
initial priority in his emergency management?
questions.explanation:
CT brain is the most important initial investigation for this gentleman who may have a sub-arachnoid haemorrhage (SAH). The cornerstone
of SAH diagnosis is the noncontrast head CT scan. The sensitivity of head CT for detecting SAH is highest in the �rst 6 to 12 hours after SAH
(nearly 100%) and then progressively declines over time to about 58% at day �ve. MRI is also sensitive but would be contraindicated because
of his pacemaker. An echocardiogram is not the most important investigation at this point, nor is a chest X-ray. A lumbar puncture would be
appropriate if the CT head was negative and there was still a high suspicion of a subarachnoid haemorrhage. (Ref: Vermeulen M, van Gijn J.
The diagnosis of subarachnoid haemorrhage. Journal of Neurology, Neurosurgery, and Psychiatry. 1990;53(5):365-372)

questions.question_text:
Mr. Gordon is a 65-year-old man who, over the past 2 years, has been making simple mistakes in his work as an accountant and has now
started to impulsively shout at his colleagues and appears very 'moody' in response to minor irritations. He does not believe there is
anything wrong with his behavior. Which of the following is most likely to be the diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to represent frontal lobe dementia as his social behaviour has coarsened, he is making errors at work, which are likely due
to executive dysfunction, and he has no insight into his di�culties. Huntington's is unlikely due to his age and lack of motor symptoms.
There is no indication of mood symptoms or memory impairment, nor is there any �uctuation in functioning.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Hornbeak is an 80-year-old woman with a diagnosis of dementia. Over the last 9 months her family has noted that she has been low in
mood and she has recently been diagnosed with a depressive episode. In which of the following dementia types is co-morbid depression
most prevalent?
questions.explanation:
Vascular dementia can be associated with depression in around 40-50% of cases. Huntington's disease and Parkinson's dementia are also
associated with increased rates of depressive illness.

questions.question_text:
Mrs. Patterson is a 66-year-old woman who has presented with evidence of dementia. She has a personal history of severe migraine and a
strong family history of stroke and early onset dementia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Mrs. Patterson is a 66-year-old
woman who has presented with evidence of dementia. She has a personal history of severe migraine and a strong family history of stroke
and early onset dementia. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis? Mrs. Patterson is a 66-year-old woman who has presented
with evidence of dementia. She has a personal history of severe migraine and a strong family history of stroke and early onset dementia.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
CADASIL (Cerebral autosomal dominant arteriopathy with subcortical infarcts and leukoencephalopthy) is an inherited condition caused by
abnormalities on the NOTCH-3 gene on the short arm of Chromosome 19. It is characterised by an autosomal dominant pattern of
inheritance with e�ected individuals experiencing migraines and then TIAs and CVAs around the age of 50 onwards. Mitochondrial
encephalomyopathy, lactic acidosis, and stroke-like episodes (MELAS) is a condition that a�ects many of the body's systems, particularly the
brain, nervous system and muscles.

questions.question_text:
Mr Tetley is an 81-year-old man who has been referred to your outpatient clinic. He and his family have noticed that he is experiencing
di�culties with his memory and has started to have unexplained falls with some rigidity. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is most likely to be dementia with Lewy Bodies in view of the early cognitive impairment and history of falls and rigidity. The other listed
disorders do have cognitive impairment as a feature, although it is often later in the course of the illness.

questions.question_text:
June Watson is a 47-year-old woman who, for the past month and since the loss of her job, has been feeling demotivated and persistently
low in mood. She describes di�culty in getting to sleep, waking at 4am most mornings, reduced interest in food, poor concentration and
low sexual energy. What's the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Moderate depression includes the two core features (low mood and anhedonia) with four or more related symptoms.

questions.question_text:
Jason is a 20-year-old man who �rst presented to mental health services with third person auditory hallucinations (running commentary)
and delusions of persecution, which lasted eight months before a more e�ective approach helped them to diminish. He has now been
relatively free of psychotic symptoms for the past nine months, except for occasional paranoia; his mother tells you that for the past three
weeks she's observed him sleeping much more than usual, he's eating little and seems to have lost motivation. You meet with him and he
tells you he's not interested in much, he's �nding it di�cult to concentrate, he's no longer enjoying the usual computer games that he used
to look forward to playing, and generally feeling quite hopeless. What the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
The diagnosis of Post schizophrenic depression is made if the patient has met general criteria for schizophrenia within the past 12 months,
with some schizophrenic symptoms remaining, and depressive symptoms having become prominent and distressing for at least 2 weeks,
ful�lling criteria for a depressive episode.

questions.question_text:
Rebecca has been struggling with symptoms of a moderate depressive illness for a few months. Her GP commenced her on Sertraline, and
she's been taking the therapeutic dose for the past two months with little improvement in her symptoms. Which of the following is the next
best course of action?

options.text: Stop all antidepressant medication and review
Switch to a di�erent class of antidepressants

questions.explanation:
Guidelines suggest switching to another SSRI. There should be a sequential trial of two SSRIs at adequate dose, for su�cient length of time,
before alternatives are considered.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Evergreen has su�ered a stroke a�ecting the dominant frontal lobe. You are asked to review her mental state and you �nd that she is
having di�culties in communicating verbally with you, although she seems to understand what you are saying. What type of speech
problem is most likely to be present given the location of the stroke?
questions.explanation: A dominant frontal lobe stroke a�ects a person's ability to produce �uent speech; language comprehension is often retained.

questions.question_text:
Valerie has had a �rst episode of depression. Her brother accompanies her to the clinic. He has a friend who has had several episodes of
depression, and wishes to know what the chances are for Valerie to go on to experience another episode of depression.
questions.explanation:
50% of those who've had a �rst episode will go on to have another, and approximately 80% of those with a history of two episodes will have
another recurrence (American Psychiatric Association 2000).

questions.question_text:
Mr Jenkins has features of mild cognitive impairment. His daughter is anxious to know what the year-on-year chances are of this progressing
to Alzheimer's dementia.
questions.explanation:
The annual adjusted conversion rate for mild cognitive impairment (MCI) to Alzheimer's dementia is 9.6%. (Acta Psychiatr Scand 2009;
119(4):252-65

questions.question_text:
Mr Kahn is a 32-year-old man with epilepsy, who has recently experienced job loss, and has had to relocate to a new area. Over the past
month he's been experiencing early morning wakening, low motivation, loss of interest in his usual hobbies, and feelings of worthlessness
and hopelessness. He wishes to start a medication with antidepressant e�ect, but is worried about what e�ect it might have on his epilepsy.
Which medication would you recommend?
questions.explanation:
SSRIs are considered �rst-line antidepressant option for patients with epilepsy. Tricyclics should be avoided, and also the dopamine and
noradrenaline-speci�c reuptake inhibitor Bupropion.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Galloway has been doing some internet research to see if she can �nd a treatment that might help her son who has longstanding
mental health di�culties. She �nds some positive literature relating to Deep Brain Stimulation and asks you about it. For what conditions
has Deep Brain Stimulation(DBS) shown to have therapeutic potential?
questions.explanation:
DBS had shown to have therapeutic potential in patients with OCD. As well as OCD, there is evidence of therapeutic e�ects for treatment-
resistant major depressive disorder, Parkinson's Disease among others.

questions.question_text:
Ted is a 36-year-old man with treatment-resistant schizophrenia who also has benign ethnic neutropenia. He has been on Clozapine for six
months, and has experienced signi�cant clinical improvement. However, his white cell count has been lowered by the use of Clozapine, and
the latest neutrophil reading was just under 1000/cubic mm. What adjunct could be considered in order to keep Ted on Clozapine and
reverse the Clozapine-induced neutropenia?
questions.explanation:
Lithium increases the white blood cell and neutrophil count, both acutely and chronically, and may be used for patients with Clozapine-
induced neutropenia (Progress in Neur and Psychiatry 2016; 20(3):13-15)

questions.question_text:
Miss Isbell is a 27-year-old woman with a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa. She is currently an informal patient on a ward. She has a BMI of
15kg/m2. In the evening she reports sudden-onset shortness-of-breath and chest pain to the nursing sta�. Which of the following is the
most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Even relative tachycardia can precipitate congestive cardiac failure in patients with anorexia nervosa and low body weight. They will often
have lost cardiac muscle and will have a relatively low heart rate. If this increases, the weakened heart cannot manage the cardiac load,
leading to pulmonary oedema and chest pain due to myocardial insu�ciency. First degree heart block is not usually associated with heart
failure. And there is nothing speci�c in the history to suggest pulmonary embolism, myocardial infarction or pneumothorax.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Arnold is a 32-year-old woman who has a known diagnosis of bipolar a�ective disorder. She is 39 weeks pregnant and has been
referred to the local Perinatal clinic for advice around her lithium. She is currently taking Priadel (Lithium carbonate) at a dose of 600mg
daily and her most recent lithium level was 0.75mmol/L. Her bipolar disorder is well controlled and she has not had a relapse for the past 2
years. Which of the following is the most appropriate plan of action?

options.text: Recheck lithium level at 5 weeks post-partum and review results at clinic one week later
Make no changes and continue usual follow-up schedule
Increase dose at delivery to 800mg and recheck lithium level after 1 week

questions.explanation:
During pregnancy GFR and plasma volume increase by around 50% and 40% respectively. These decrease again rapidly after delivery. A
higher lithium dose is often necessary during the thirds trimester as a result. However, these changes rapidly reverse following delivery,
which could pose a high risk of toxicity in the mother. But stopping it abruptly risks a relapse, particularly in a mother with a history of
bipolar a�ective disorder, who could have a 50% chance of becoming acutely ill following delivery. As the patient's lithium level is well within
the recommended maintenance range (0.4-1.0mmol/L) then it is reasonable to reduce the dose to 400mg prior to delivery. Lithium should
be stopped when labour starts and the mother's levels checked 12 hours after her last dose. It can then be restarted following delivery and
the levels checked regularly. It is advised that women do not breastfeed when taking lithium as it is transferred into the milk in signi�cant
concentrations.

questions.question_text:
Mr Oliver Hirsh is a 24-year-old man who has a diagnosis of paranoid schizophrenia. He was brought to A&E by his family after he presented
as confused at home. In A&E he was found to be hyperthermic, tachycardic, hypertensive and showing signs of increased muscular re�exes.
He managed to inform the sta� that he took an overdose of Sertraline and Haloperidol earlier that day. Which of the following is the most
likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
This is more likely to be Serotonin syndrome as the patient is presenting with rapid onset symptoms and hyperre�exia. Neuroleptic
malignant syndrome is associated with onset of symptoms over the course of days to weeks and characterized by muscular rigidity.
Anticholinergic toxicity is associated with profound visual impairment, urinary retention and marked constipation.

questions.question_text:
Mr Keith Viner is a 38-year-old man who has presented to his GP with a 6 week history of low mood, poor motivation, diminished sleep and
appetite, limited energy levels and feelings of despair about the future. He is willing to try medication but has heard that some psychiatric
medications can cause sexual side-e�ects, which he is keen to avoid. Which of the following are least likely to cause sexual side-e�ects?
questions.explanation:
Mirtazapine, Bupropion and Vortioxetine are the antidepressants least associated with sexual side-e�ects. Fewer than 10% of patients
taking Mirtazapine report di�culties. Around 70% of those taking SSRIs or Venlafaxine report symptoms. TCAs are signi�cantly associated
with sexual side-e�ects as well.

questions.question_text:
In your outpatient clinic you are seeing Miss Jackson, a 30-year-old teacher experiencing her �rst episode of depression. She has been
prescribed 40mg citalopram for 2 months with some improvement in sleep and appetite but she continues to have negative ruminations,
anxiety, suicidal thoughts, and is unable to concentrate and work. She has not had any other treatments for depression. She is on the
waiting list for CBT but this will likely not be available for some months. Which ONE of the following pharmacological treatments should you
o�er her today?

options.text: Switch to a di�erent SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor)

correct_answer.text: Switch to a di�erent SSRI (selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor)

questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines recommend that when reviewing drug treatment for a person whose symptoms have not responded to initial
pharmacological interventions consideration should be given to switching to an alternative antidepressant. Checking compliance prior to
doing this is also important. NICE Guideline (CG90) 1.8.1.2 states: Consider switching to: initially a di�erent SSRI or a better tolerated newer-
generation antidepressant, subsequently an antidepressant of a di�erent pharmacological class that may be less well tolerated, for example
venlafaxine, a TCA or an MAOI Augmentation with another agent would not be appropriate initially but may be required if other treatments
are not successful. The maximum dose for citalopram is 40mg so increasing to 60mg is not advised, due to the risk of QT prolongation.
(Reference: Depression in adults: recognition and management, Clinical guideline [CG90]

questions.question_text:
Mr Jenkins is a 20-year-old man who is being reviewed in �rst seizure clinic. The neurologist suspects he su�ers from non-epileptic attacks
(or dissociative seizures) based on the history Mr Jenkins provides. Which ONE of the following patient reported seizure characteristics has
the best utility in di�erentiating non-epileptic attacks from epilepsy?

options.text: Biting the inside of the mouth
Recall for the period of unresponsiveness

correct_answer.text: Recall for the period of unresponsiveness

questions.explanation:
Although patients with Non-Epileptic Attacks (NEA) often report seizures in sleep, when they are captured on telemetry they are inevitably
preceded by waking, which again can be recorded electrographically. Thus patient report of seizures during sleep are not necessarily helpful
as discriminators and need to be examined further. The following are also not de�nitive discriminators: Biting the inside of the mouth occurs
occasionally in NEA and commonly in epilepsy. Incontinence can occasionally occur in NEA and occurs commonly in epilepsy. Stereotyped
attacks occur commonly in both NEA and epilepsy. Patients with NEA often have recall for their period of apparent unresponsiveness,
whereas those with epileptic seizures do not. Therefore of the above list, this is the best answer. (Reference: Mellers JD. The approach to
patients with "non-epileptic seizures“. Postgraduate medical journal. 2005 Aug 1;81(958):498-504).

questions.question_text:
Neurosurgery for mental disorders (NMD) is an uncommon treatment modality. NICE has suggested it in certain circumstances. Which of
the following disorders can be treated with NMD according to NICE guidelines?
questions.explanation:
Intractable OCD can be treated via neurosurgery if other treatment modalities have failed. NMD is rarely performed with only 4 procedures
carried out in 2015-16.

questions.question_text:
Miss Di�orio is a 39-year-old woman who is having outpatient treatment for her stable bipolar illness. She has read recently about gender
di�erences in mental health conditions and would like to know more about this with relevance to bipolar. Which ONE of the following
bipolar spectrum conditions or comorbidities has an equal gender distribution?
questions.explanation:
Previous studies and a review in 2010 report an almost equal gender ratio in the prevalence of bipolar disorder but the majority of studies
do report an increased risk in women of bipolar II/hypomania, rapid cycling and mixed a�ective episodes. Comorbidity; particularly thyroid
disease, migraine, obesity, and anxiety disorders occur more frequently in women than men, whilst substance use disorders are more
common in men. (References: Di�orio A, Jones I. Is sex important? Gender di�erences in bipolar disorder. International Review of Psychiatry.
2010 Oct 1;22(5):437-52. Arnold LM. Gender di�erences in bipolar disorder. The Psychiatric Clinics of North America. 2003 Sep;26(3):595-
620).

questions.question_text:
Miss Olivia Hunt is a 33-year-old woman with a diagnosis of obsessive compulsive disorder. She has recently received an adequate trial of
Sertraline 200mg daily and a course of CBT for 20 sessions. Unfortunately, this has made little di�erence to her symptoms. Which of the
following would be the most appropriate next step in her management?
questions.explanation:
The NICE guidelines indicate that if a patient has had an adequate trial of a combined SSRI and CBT then they should be o�ered a di�erent
SSRI or Clomipramine. If this is ine�ective, then further intensive CBT or a low dose antipsychotic can be o�ered.

questions.question_text:
John is 26 years old and has body dysmorphic disorder (BDD). He has been taking sertraline 200mg for the last three months and having
CBT but continues to spend hours of the day looking in the mirror. He has previously tried �uoxetine at maximum dose with minimal
bene�t. What is the best next step in treatment?

options.text: Switch from sertraline to another SSRI

questions.explanation:
NICE guidelines state BDD should be treated initially with CBT and then if symptoms are severe adding an SSRI. There is very limited
research on head to head trials for antidepressants or for treatment resistant BDD. The Maudsley guidelines suggest that buspirone may
augment the SSRI. (Ref: NICE Guidelines: Obsessive-compulsive disorder and body dysmorphic disorder: treatment. Clinical guideline [CG31]
(2005). Available: Taylor, D., Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Anxiety Spectrum Disorders. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th ed. Chichester:
John Wiley & Sons, pp.355).

questions.question_text:
You are seeing a 25-year-old woman in outpatients for treatment of moderate depression. Which ONE of the following symptoms are
considered a core feature of depression?
questions.explanation:
A study of outpatients with either or major depression found that across all levels of severity some symptoms were present in 60% or more
of patients. The following are therefore considered core symptoms: Sad, irritable, or anxious mood, Loss of interest or pleasure, Impaired
concentration and decision making, Worthlessness and inappropriate guilt, Hopelessness, Fatigue or loss of energy. Panic attacks may occur
in depression with anxiety but are not a core feature. Talkativeness would suggest hypomania or mania. Auditory hallucinations can occur in
psychotic depression but are not a core feature of depression. All over body pain can occur in depression, especially in particular ethnic
groups but is not an agreed core symptom according to current criteria. (Ref: Rakofsky JJ, Schettler PJ, Kinkead BL, Frank E, Judd LL, Kupfer
DJ, Rush AJ, Thase ME, Yonkers KA, Rapaport MH. The prevalence and severity of depressive symptoms along the spectrum of unipolar
depressive disorders: a post hoc analysis. The Journal of clinical psychiatry. 2013 Nov;74(11):1084-91)

questions.question_text:
Mr Fox is a 60-year-old man who is taking lithium for stable bipolar disorder. He presents to A&E with confusion and falls in the context of a
recent chest infection. Which of the following features would be NOT be consistent with acute lithium toxicity?
questions.explanation:
Nystagmus, ataxia, sluggishness, agitation, fasciculations and coarse tremor are neurological features of lithium toxicity. Reported cardiac
e�ects are QTc prolongation and bradycardia. Fever is not seen in lithium toxicity and would suggest sepsis or the need to consider
neuroleptic malignant syndrome, depending on the other symptoms. (Ref: Perrone J, Chatterjee P. Lithium poisoning.  uptodate.
com. Wolters Kluwer Health. 2015:1-3)

questions.question_text:
Mrs Carol Anwar is a 40-year-old woman who has a diagnosis of HIV and a history of having di�culty taking her antiretrovirals regularly. She
has been admitted to A&E in a confused and feverish state. Her MRI scan shows multiple ring-enhancing lesions. Which of the following is
the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation:
Multiple ring enhancing lesions on MRI in patients with a diagnosis of HIV tend to indicate either CNS toxoplasmosis or CNS lymphoma. The
two are generally distinguished by CT scan.

questions.question_text:
Mrs Tara Neville is a 32-year-old woman with a diagnosis of schizophrenia. She has been well for 3 years and she and her husband are
planning on having children. She is wondering what the risk of them developing schizophrenia would be. Which of the following would be
the most appropriate answer?
questions.explanation: Studies indicate that children have a risk of around 9-14% of developing schizophrenia if one of their parents has the diagnosis.

questions.question_text:
A young male patient on the acute psychiatric ward is known to have non-epileptic attacks. After a ward round he is observed in the
common area on the sofa with jerky movements and appearing to have an attack. Which ONE the following features are more likely to
suggest that this is an epileptic rather than a non-epileptic attack?

options.text: Resistance to eye opening during the attack
Side to side head movements during attack
Evidence of visual �xation during the attack
Downgoing plantar re�exes after the attack
Impaired ability to recall the attack

correct_answer.text: Impaired ability to recall the attack

questions.explanation:
Side to side head movements and resistance to eye opening are more common in Non-Epileptic Attacks. Neurological testing during a Non-
Epileptic Attack will �nd that visual �xation is present (whereas it is not in an epileptic attack). Plantars are often up-going after an epileptic
attack and should be normal after a non-Epileptic Attack. Inability to recall the attack and post-ictal confusion is suggestive of an epileptic
attack. (Ref: Mellers JD. The approach to patients with "non-epileptic seizures“. Postgraduate medical journal. 2005 Aug 1;81(958):498-504)

questions.question_text:
Which ONE mood-stabilizing medication used in bipolar is associated with the greatest reduction in risk of attempted and completed
suicide?
questions.explanation:
Around 15% of people with bipolar complete suicide. Meta-analyses of clinical trials have demonstrated that lithium reduced the risk of both
attempted and completed suicide. Two large database studies have shown that patients taking lithium were less likely to complete suicide
than those treated with valproate, valproic acid or other mood stabilizing drugs such as gapabentin or carbamazepine. (Ref: Taylor, D.,
Paton, C. and Kapur, S. (n.d.). Chapter 3: Bipolar a�ective disorder. The Maudsley prescribing guidelines in psychiatry. 12th ed. Chichester:
John Wiley & Sons, pp.190)

questions.question_text:
Numerous risk factors have been identi�ed for the development of schizophrenia. Which of the following is most likely to place an individual
at risk of developing schizophrenia?

questions.question_text:
